_comment: Targeted relevance cases (same shape as adversarial_cases.json). 'reject:*' cases are demonstrable contradictions of an established lifecycle stage or a verified-absent declaration. 'accept' cases are qualified, historical, rule-out or unfamiliar-but-supported statements that must NOT be rejected: they pin the absence of false-positive rejections. A generic explanation that contradicts nothing is accepted by design; see NOTES.md for the remaining relevance limitations.

cases.possible: The pod may not be schedulable because no node currently has enough capacity for it.
The pod may be unschedulable because a node taint is not tolerated.
The scheduler may have failed to place the pod on any node, which could explain why it is not running.
A node scheduling constraint may not explain this, since the pod was scheduled. The image tag may not exist in the registry, which could explain why the pull fails.
Scheduling may not explain this, because the pod was placed on a node. The registry may have rejected the credentials used for the pull, which could explain the failure.
The pod may have been briefly unschedulable earlier, but it is now placed on a node and the image pull is what currently fails.
The image tag may not exist in the registry, which could explain why the pull fails.
A registry rate limit or an expired pull credential may be causing the image pull to fail.
The pod may be unschedulable because no node has enough allocatable memory for its request.
The container may have restarted because its entrypoint command is incorrect.
The container image may be unsuitable for this workload, which could explain the earlier restart.
A failing health probe may have caused Kubernetes to restart the container.
An unhandled exception in the application may have crashed the container.
The container may have exceeded its 128Mi memory limit and been OOMKilled.
A memory leak in the application may have grown the process until it reached the memory limit, which could explain the earlier termination.
A burst of large requests may have raised the container's memory use past its limit before it recovered.
The entrypoint may not be the cause. The container may have been OOMKilled, which is a memory event.
Earlier restarts may have come from an incorrect startup command, in addition to the recorded out-of-memory kill.
The readiness probe may be failing, which could explain why the container is not ready.
The liveness probe may be killing the container, which could explain the restarts.
The readiness probe may be failing, which could explain why the container is not ready.
The container may have started but is not responding to readiness probes, which could mean the application is not ready to serve traffic.
The pod may not be schedulable due to a node selector or affinity constraint.
A node selector may not be the reason the pod is Pending; an untolerated node taint may explain it.
The container may be configured with an insufficient memory request, leading to frequent OOMKilled events despite the limit being set to 128Mi.
The container may have been restarted due to a resource request mismatch, such as a misconfigured memory limit.
The earlier OOMKilled termination may have been caused by an insufficient memory request, while the limit is 128Mi.
The memory request and limit may both be too low for the workload, which could explain the earlier OOMKilled termination.
The container's memory request is 64Mi and its limit is 128Mi, which may not be sufficient for the workload, leading to OOMKilled terminations.
The earlier OOMKilled termination may not be caused by the memory request; the container may have exceeded its 128Mi limit.
A low memory request may make this pod an earlier eviction victim under node memory pressure, separately from the OOMKilled termination.
